title: JavaScript and Node.js security
summary: How JavaScript fails on servers and desktops: prototype pollution, ReDoS on the event loop, node:vm escapes, child_process and deserialisation bugs, npm in-process risk, SSR trust and Electron.
outcomes: Explain why one blocked callback or one polluted prototype affects every user of a Node.js process
Trace a prototype pollution bug from source to gadget to sink, and fix it with own-key checks, Map or null-prototype objects
Spot regular expressions that backtrack catastrophically, measure them with near-miss inputs and rewrite or bound them
Explain why node:vm and vm2 are not security boundaries, and choose process or isolate boundaries instead
Call child processes without shell or option injection, including the Windows batch-file case
Analyse React2Shell and the Next.js middleware bypass as trust failures and apply the fixes
Review an Electron app's webPreferences, preload bridge, IPC handlers, navigation rules and fuses
Plan detections and a response for JavaScript-specific attacks: process trees, event-loop health, request content and runtime guardrails

lessons.title: One thread for every request: how Node.js runs JavaScript

blocks.md:
JavaScript was built to run inside web pages, where the browser keeps it in a box: the same-origin policy and the renderer sandbox you met in the browser security model course. **Node.js** takes the same language out of the box. The Node.js project describes it as an asynchronous, event-driven JavaScript runtime: a program that runs JavaScript files on a server or a laptop, with access to files, the network and other processes.

Two parts do the work. **V8**, Google's open source JavaScript and WebAssembly engine (also used in Chrome), compiles and runs the code. **libuv**, a support library focused on asynchronous I/O (input and output), waits on sockets and files for it. Most server frameworks you will see, such as Express (a minimal web framework for Node.js) and Next.js (a framework from the company Vercel for React, Meta's user-interface library), run on top of Node.js.

The key fact for security is how Node.js handles many users at once. The official guide *Don't Block the Event Loop* says there are two kinds of threads: **one Event Loop** (also called the main thread) and a small **Worker Pool** of k threads in libuv for expensive tasks such as file I/O, DNS lookups, some crypto and compression.

The Event Loop runs every JavaScript callback: the function that handles request A, then the one for request B, then A's database reply. It is fast because each callback is short. The guide spells out the consequence: if one callback spends too long, "all current and new clients will not get a turn".

blocks.title: Three requests share one Event Loop

scenes.caption: Request A arrives. Its handler runs on the Event Loop for 2 ms and asks for a file, which libuv hands to the Worker Pool.
While A's file is read, the loop is free, so B and C get their turns. Short callbacks let one thread serve many clients.
A's file is ready, so A's next callback runs. Nobody waited more than a few milliseconds.
Now request X carries input that makes its handler compute for 25 ms. B and C arrive during it and cannot start. Simplified: real timings vary, the queueing does not.

blocks.md: You can watch this happen with two timers. The second one simulates a request handler that does 300 ms of synchronous work (work that never yields back to the loop). The first timer was due after 10 ms, but it has to wait its turn.

blocks.caption: Run on Node.js 22. The 10 ms timer ran 294 ms late because the only thread that runs JavaScript was busy.

blocks.md:
The guide names the security consequence directly: if some input makes a thread block, "a malicious client could submit this 'evil input', make your threads block, and keep them from working on other clients", which is a denial of service (DoS). Lessons 7 and 8 are about the most common evil input, regular expressions.

A second consequence: **every request shares one process**. Objects, caches, global variables and loaded modules live as long as the process. If one request can change shared state, the change affects every later request, including other users'. Lessons 2 to 6 are about the most JavaScript-specific way to do that, prototype pollution.

**What Node.js trusts.** The project's security policy (SECURITY.md in the nodejs/node repository) lists what Node.js does *not* trust: data from the remote end of network connections, such as HTTP requests, and the content of files it reads. It trusts everything else, including "the code it is asked to run, including JavaScript, WASM and native code", which explicitly covers "all dependencies installed from the npm registry". That code "inherits all the privileges of the execution user".

So a Node.js process has no internal walls. Your code, every npm package and anything an attacker manages to run all share one heap, one set of globals and the full rights of the operating system user. Browser JavaScript is boxed by origin; server JavaScript is boxed only by the operating system.

Node.js runs all JavaScript for all users on one Event Loop in one process with the user's full privileges. That gives JavaScript servers two bug classes that matter more than elsewhere: input that blocks the loop (denial of service for everyone) and input that changes shared objects (a change that persists for every later request).

"Async" does not mean "parallel". `async` functions and promises still run their JavaScript on the Event Loop; only waiting (for the network, a file, a timer) happens elsewhere. A slow loop inside an `async` handler blocks every other user exactly like a slow loop anywhere else.

blocks.question: A Node.js API handler runs a CPU-heavy calculation that takes 2 seconds for certain inputs. What do other users of the same process experience during those 2 seconds?
options: Nothing: each request runs on its own thread from the Worker Pool
Only users of the same endpoint wait; other routes keep working
Their requests wait, because all JavaScript callbacks run on the single Event Loop
The calculation is paused automatically after 100 ms so others can run
blocks.explain: JavaScript callbacks all run on the one Event Loop. The Worker Pool handles specific expensive APIs (file I/O, DNS, some crypto, compression), not your handler's JavaScript. Node.js never preempts a running callback, and routes do not get separate threads, so every client waits.

blocks.question: Which of these does the Node.js threat model treat as trusted?
options: A package installed from the npm registry and loaded with require()
The body of an incoming HTTP request
A response received from a remote server over an outbound connection
Bytes read from a file the application opened
blocks.explain: SECURITY.md treats network data in both directions and file contents as untrusted, but trusts the code it is asked to run, explicitly including npm dependencies. A malicious package is therefore never a Node.js vulnerability: it already runs with the user's full privileges.

lessons.title: Prototypes: where a missing property comes from

blocks.md:
Create an empty object in JavaScript, `const o = {}`, and ask for `o.toString`. You get a function, although you never added one. MDN Web Docs (Mozilla's developer documentation) explains why: every object has a reference to a **prototype**, another object; when a property is not on the object itself, the runtime looks in the prototype, then the prototype's prototype, and so on, until it finds the property or reaches an object whose prototype is `null`. That path is the **prototype chain**.

For ordinary objects made with `{}` or `JSON.parse`, the chain is short: the object, then `Object.prototype`, then `null`. A `Set` goes `Set.prototype`, then `Object.prototype`. So `Object.prototype` sits at the end of almost every chain in the program.

blocks.title: Looking up a property that is not there

scenes.caption: user has one own property, name. Its prototype is Object.prototype, which holds shared methods such as toString.
name is found on the object itself, so the lookup stops immediately.
toString is not on user, so the runtime walks one step up the chain and finds it on Object.prototype.
isAdmin is on neither object, and Object.prototype's prototype is null, so the answer is undefined. Code that checks if (user.isAdmin) treats this as false.
One assignment adds isAdmin to the shared prototype. Nothing about user changed.
Now the same lookup finds isAdmin one step up the chain, for user and for every other ordinary object, including ones created later.
Object.hasOwn asks only about the object itself. It still says false: the value is inherited, not owned.

blocks.md:
Two property names reach the prototype instead of naming an ordinary property:

- `__proto__` is an **accessor** on `Object.prototype` (a property backed by getter and setter functions rather than a stored value). Reading `o.__proto__` returns the prototype; assigning to it changes which object is the prototype. MDN marks it deprecated, but it still works in browsers and Node.js.
- `constructor` is an ordinary inherited property: `({}).constructor` is the `Object` function, and `Object.prototype` hangs off it. So `o.constructor.prototype` is the same object as `Object.getPrototypeOf(o)`.

A third tool removes the chain: `Object.create(null)` makes an object whose prototype is `null`. It has no `toString`, no `__proto__` accessor and no `constructor`, so nothing can be reached through it.

Here is the surprising part. In JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, the text format for data), `__proto__` is just a key. `JSON.parse` creates an **own** property with that name and does not touch any prototype. An object literal written in code with the same text does set the prototype. PortSwigger, the company behind the Burp Suite web testing tool, uses exactly this comparison in its Web Security Academy:

blocks.caption: The parsed object a just has a key called __proto__. The literal b got a new prototype. Neither touched Object.prototype.

blocks.prompt: `options` comes from `JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"test": "value"}}')`. The code then runs `const withDefaults = Object.assign({ mode: "cors" }, options)`. What do `withDefaults.test` and `({}).test` print?
blocks.reveal: `withDefaults.test` prints `value` and `({}).test` prints `undefined`. MDN uses this example: `Object.assign` copies each own key with an ordinary assignment, so copying the key `__proto__` runs `withDefaults.__proto__ = { test: "value" }`, which calls the setter and swaps `withDefaults`'s prototype. Object.prototype itself is untouched, because only one level of `__proto__` was involved. We ran it on Node.js 22 and got exactly that. The lesson: JSON input is safe to parse, but *copying* its keys onto other objects can reach prototypes. Two levels deep, as the next lesson shows, reaches the shared one.

blocks.md: Reading a missing property silently falls through to the prototype chain, ending at Object.prototype, which nearly every object shares. The keys `__proto__` and `constructor` (then `prototype`) lead from an ordinary object to that shared object. `Object.create(null)` objects have no chain to follow.

blocks.question: Which statement about `JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"x": 1}}')` is correct?
options: It immediately sets Object.prototype.x to 1
It throws, because __proto__ is a reserved key in JSON
It returns an object whose prototype is { x: 1 }
It returns an object with an own property named __proto__; no prototype changes until code copies that key elsewhere
blocks.explain: JSON.parse defines keys as own data properties, so __proto__ is just a name there (Object.keys shows it). Danger starts when later code assigns that key onto another object, for example in a merge or Object.assign, because assignment triggers the __proto__ setter.

lessons.title: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object

blocks.md:
**Prototype pollution** is, in MDN's words, a vulnerability where an attacker can add or modify properties on an object's prototype, so that malicious values unexpectedly appear on objects throughout the application. The word comes from older JavaScript slang: security researcher Olivier Arteau's paper for NorthSec 2018 (a security conference in Montreal) *Prototype pollution attack in NodeJS application* notes the term was coined long before to describe libraries that added methods to built-in prototypes, a practice soon considered bad. Arteau asked what happens when an *attacker* can do it.

MDN gives the code shape behind it: a dynamic property write `obj[key1][key2] = value` where the keys come from input. If `key1` is `__proto__`, then `obj[key1]` *is* Object.prototype, and the write lands there. The most common sources are a hand-written deep merge and, our example here, property definition by path, both on Arteau's list.

Many apps accept nested settings as dotted paths, such as a form field named `theme.color`, and a helper walks the path, creating objects as needed. Here is a typical helper, and what happens when a field name is `__proto__.isAdmin`:

blocks.caption: Vulnerable. The second call writes to Object.prototype, so an unrelated object created later reports isAdmin true without owning it.

blocks.title: Where setPath writes for each path

scenes.caption: Normal path theme.color. The walk starts at prefs; prefs.theme is undefined, so the helper creates a new object there and writes color on it. Only prefs changed.
Crafted path __proto__.isAdmin. prefs['__proto__'] is not undefined: the accessor returns Object.prototype, so the helper steps into the shared prototype instead of creating anything.
The last key is written where the walk ended: Object.prototype.isAdmin = true.
A user object created later in another module owns only name, yet user.isAdmin is true by inheritance. So is every other ordinary object in the process, for every later request.

blocks.md:
**The second route.** MDN points out that even with `__proto__` disabled, `constructor.prototype` reaches the same object. We tested both routes against the helper above, with and without Node.js's `--disable-proto=delete` flag, which deletes the `__proto__` accessor at start-up (its sibling mode `throw` makes any use of it throw an error with code `ERR_PROTO_ACCESS`).

- `__proto__.isAdmin`: polluted with plain `node`; not polluted with `--disable-proto=delete`.
- `constructor.prototype.isAdmin`: polluted with plain `node`; **still polluted** with `--disable-proto=delete`.

With the accessor deleted, `prefs['__proto__']` is just undefined, so the helper creates an ordinary own property named `__proto__`: harmless. The `constructor` route needs no accessor at all.

**Where these sinks hide.** Arteau's paper groups the vulnerable operations into three families: recursive **merge** (deep-copying one object into another), **property definition by path** (like `setPath`, or `_.set` in utility libraries), and **clone** (often implemented as a merge into an empty object). MDN adds a fourth that is easy to miss: query-string parsers that build nested objects from names such as `a[b]=1` or `a.b=1`. MDN also notes why libraries are more exposed than application code: a generic library cannot allowlist the keys it will see.

blocks.caption: Fixed. Three independent changes; each one alone keeps Object.prototype clean, and together they also stop a crafted path from swapping prefs's own prototype and survive a future edit that forgets one.

blocks.md:
Why each change works:

1. **Refusing the three names.** These are the only keys that lead from an ordinary object to a prototype, so this short denylist is complete for that purpose. It is not guessing at attacker spellings.
2. **`Object.hasOwn` instead of `=== undefined`.** The helper now steps only into objects the target really owns; an inherited value is never treated as a place to write.
3. **`Object.create(null)` containers.** The objects the helper creates, and `prefs` itself, have no prototype at all, so there is nothing for `__proto__` or `constructor` to reach.

`--disable-proto` is a useful second layer, not the fix: our test shows the `constructor.prototype` route still pollutes with it on. Fix the write (own keys, refused names, null-prototype objects); add the flag as defence in depth.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: find every place an input-controlled key is used in a write, every set-by-path, merge, clone and nested query parser, and every library that provides them; apply the fix above or use a `Map` (next lessons). *Detect*: request bodies, query strings or form field names containing `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype` are rarely legitimate and are cheap to log and alert on. *Respond*: pollution lives in the process's memory until it exits, so restart affected processes after the fix, then review logs for which requests carried those keys.

blocks.question: A code reviewer sees `target[k1][k2] = v` where `k1` and `k2` come from a JSON body. The team proposes rejecting only the key `__proto__`. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: __proto__ is the only way to reach Object.prototype
k1 = constructor and a deeper write via prototype still reach Object.prototype; refuse all three names or use own-key checks and null-prototype objects
JSON.parse already removes __proto__, so the check is redundant
The check must be case-insensitive because JavaScript property names ignore case
blocks.explain: MDN describes the constructor.prototype route explicitly, and our test showed it working even with --disable-proto=delete. JSON.parse keeps __proto__ as an own key rather than removing it, and property names are case-sensitive.

blocks.question: Why does pollution of a Node.js server's Object.prototype affect users other than the attacker?
options: Because the polluted value is written into each user's session cookie
Because Object.prototype is shared by ordinary objects across the whole process, and the process serves every user until it restarts
Because Node.js copies prototypes to every worker thread on each request
It does not: each request gets a fresh Object.prototype
blocks.explain: All requests to one Node.js process share the same heap and the same built-in prototypes (lesson 1). A property added to Object.prototype by one request is inherited by objects created for every later request, until the process exits.

lessons.title: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)

blocks.md:
Gadgets range from mild to severe. From MDN and PortSwigger:

- **Logic.** `if (!user.isAdmin) deny()` where non-admins simply lack the property: pollution makes everyone an admin.
- **Request options.** MDN shows `fetch(url, { mode: "cors" })` turning into a POST with an attacker's body once `method` and `body` are polluted.
- **Behaviour you can observe safely.** PortSwigger's server-side techniques include Express's `json spaces` setting, which controls JSON indentation and is usually left undefined; polluting it visibly changes response formatting. PortSwigger notes this was fixed in Express 4.17.4. Testers use such harmless signals because, as PortSwigger warns, real server-side pollution persists for the process lifetime and can easily take the server down.
- **Process spawning.** Options for starting child processes, such as `env`, `shell` and `execArgv` (extra command-line arguments for a new Node.js process), are classic gadgets, because each one changes what program runs or how.

**Real case: Kibana, CVE-2019-7609.** Kibana is the web interface of the company Elastic for exploring data stored in Elasticsearch, Elastic's search and analytics database. Elastic's advisory ESA-2019-02 (19 February 2019) described "an arbitrary code execution flaw in the Timelion visualizer" (Timelion was Kibana's tool for charting time series with a small expression language) in versions before 5.6.15 and 6.6.1, exploitable by anyone with access to Timelion. The advisory did not say *how*.

Michał Bentkowski, chief security researcher at the Polish penetration testing firm Securitum, published the root cause in October 2019. Timelion's `props` function let an expression set nested properties on a chart, for example a label path like `label.x`. A path through `__proto__` therefore wrote to Object.prototype: a path-style source exactly like lesson 3's `setPath`.

Finding a gadget took longer. Bentkowski noticed that another Kibana feature started a new Node.js child process, and that Node.js's internal `normalizeSpawnArguments` read `options.env` and, when it was undefined, fell back to the parent's environment. Kibana never set `env`, so a polluted `env` became the child's whole environment.

Environment variables are powerful for Node.js: `NODE_OPTIONS` passes command-line options to every Node.js process that starts. Bentkowski used it to make the new process load code the attacker controlled, giving commands with the rights of the Kibana process. Elastic's workaround for those who could not upgrade was to set `timelion.enabled: false`. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2019-7609 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 10 January 2022, meaning it had been seen exploited in the wild.

scenes.caption: Source: a Timelion expression sets a nested property, and a path through __proto__ lands on Object.prototype.
Nothing happens yet. The pollution waits in memory until some code reads a property it never set.
Gadget: another feature starts a Node.js child process without an env option, so the spawn code looks env up and finds the polluted one on the prototype.
Sink: the child starts with the attacker's environment. NODE_OPTIONS changes how Node.js starts, which was enough to run the attacker's code with Kibana's rights.

blocks.md: **Node.js hardened this gadget, years later.** In July 2023 Node.js merged [pull request 48726](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/48726), *child_process: harden against prototype pollution*, so that spawn options such as `cwd`, `env`, `shell` and `execArgv` are not taken from the prototype. A follow-up by developer Liran Tal, [pull request 53781](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/53781) (July 2024), fixed cases the first change missed in `spawn()`, `spawnSync()` and `execFileSync()`, and its description notes this "is not considered a security vulnerability" because the Node.js threat model leaves prototype pollution to the application. We checked on Node.js 22:

blocks.caption: On a current Node.js, a polluted env or shell is ignored by child_process. Library and application gadgets are not covered by this hardening.

blocks.md: Do not read the hardening as "pollution is solved". It closes gadgets inside Node.js's own child_process code only. Your framework, template engine, HTTP client and your own options objects are full of optional properties, and every one is a possible gadget. The fix is still to stop pollution at the source.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: fix sources (lesson 3); keep frameworks and Node.js patched, because gadget fixes ship as ordinary releases (Express closed its json spaces gadget in 4.17.4). *Detect*: an endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent or Linux audit rules (auditd, the kernel's audit system, logging every program start) see the sink, not the pollution: a Node.js service starting a shell or a second `node` process with an unusual environment, or `NODE_OPTIONS` appearing in a child's environment, is a strong signal. In web logs look for `__proto__` and `constructor` in bodies. *Respond*: restart every process that could have been polluted, then treat the host as compromised if a spawn gadget was reachable.

blocks.question: Which property is the best candidate for a prototype pollution gadget?
options: A property the code always assigns in the object literal it creates
A method defined on a class prototype that every instance overrides
A property read only through Object.hasOwn checks
An optional property of an options object that the code reads but usually leaves undefined, then uses to decide what to run
blocks.explain: Polluted values are only seen when the object lacks its own property, so always-assigned properties cannot be gadgets. Optional settings with dangerous uses, such as env or shell for spawning, are the classic gadgets. Object.hasOwn ignores inherited values, which is why it is a defence.

blocks.question: After upgrading to a Node.js release that includes pull requests 48726 and 53781, a team decides their unpatched deep-merge helper is no longer a risk. Why is that wrong?
options: The pull requests hardened only Node.js's own child_process option handling; other gadgets in frameworks, libraries and the app still read polluted properties
Those changes only apply when Node.js runs with --permission
The changes were reverted because the Node.js threat model rejects them
Prototype pollution only matters in browsers, so the helper was never a risk
blocks.explain: The hardening stops child_process from reading env, shell and similar options from the prototype. Logic gadgets (isAdmin), request options, template engine options and countless library defaults are untouched. The source still has to be fixed.

lessons.title: Client-side prototype pollution: from a URL to DOM XSS

blocks.md: PortSwigger's model gadget is a library that reads a configuration object and loads a script from a URL in it. The developer never sets `transport_url`, so the library falls back to the prototype:

blocks.caption: If anything pollutes Object.prototype.transport_url, the vulnerable version loads a script from wherever it points. The fixed version ignores inherited values and allowlists the origin. Under enforced Trusted Types, run that origin check inside a policy's createScriptURL instead.

blocks.title: From a crafted link to a foreign script

scenes.caption: The victim opens a link to the real site. Its query string contains a parameter whose name walks through __proto__.
The page's query parser turns parameter names into nested objects and writes through __proto__: Object.prototype.transport_url now exists.
Later the library builds its config. transport_url is not set, so the lookup falls through to the prototype.
The script tag points at the attacker's host and runs in the site's origin: DOM XSS from a URL parameter.

With a nonce plus strict-dynamic CSP the GET above still happens: trust passes to scripts a trusted script creates. Enforced Trusted Types stop it one step earlier: assigning a plain string to script.src throws, so no request is sent.

blocks.md:
**Finding it.** DOM Invader is PortSwigger's browser-based testing tool, available only in Burp Suite's built-in browser. Its documentation says the prototype pollution mode, off by default to avoid breaking sites, automatically detects pollution sources in the URL and in JSON sent through web messages, can pollute Object.prototype to prove a source, and scans for gadgets. Manually, a tester adds a harmless property through a candidate source and checks in the console whether `({}).thatProperty` exists.

**Browser APIs as gadgets.** MDN lists configuration objects as the most sensitive targets: `fetch` options (method, body, headers), the `srcdoc` property of an iframe, and sanitizer configuration objects. A sanitizer such as DOMPurify (taught in the client-side course) that reads an option from an inherited property could be told to allow tags it should strip.

The client-side fixes are the same as on the server: null-prototype objects or `Map` for parsed parameters, `Object.hasOwn` before trusting an option, refuse `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` keys in parsers and merges, and keep third-party parsers patched. A strict CSP still blocks gadgets that inject inline script or handlers, but 'strict-dynamic' trusts a script a trusted library creates, as here. Enforced Trusted Types close that gap: a polluted string cannot reach `script.src`.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: audit URL and message parsers your pages use (including small ones bundled inside libraries), and freeze the prototype early if your code allows it (next lesson). Enforce Trusted Types (`require-trusted-types-for 'script'`), starting in report-only mode. *Detect*: Trusted Types violation reports (sent through CSP reporting) are the clearest signal, because the server never sees the polluting part if it is in the URL fragment. A strict-dynamic policy reports nothing here, since it lets scripts created by trusted scripts load. *Respond*: ship the parser fix, then look at CSP reports and referrers to find the crafted links that were circulating.

blocks.question: A page reads `location.hash`, parses it into nested objects, and later calls a widget with `{}` as its options. Server logs show nothing unusual. Why might this still be exploitable, and why are the logs blind to it?
options: It is not exploitable: prototype pollution needs a server
The server strips __proto__ from all URLs automatically
The fragment is never sent to the server, so the polluting input and the gadget both run only in the browser
Browsers ignore prototype changes made from the fragment
blocks.explain: The URL fragment stays in the browser (recall the DOM XSS lesson), so a hash parser can pollute the page's Object.prototype without any server request containing the payload. Detection must come from the browser side: CSP reports and client-side testing.

lessons.title: Defending against prototype pollution at every layer

blocks.md:
MDN groups the defences into two lines: avoid code that can turn into prototype modifications, and avoid reading properties that might have been polluted. A third line removes the target. We will go from the most targeted fix to the broadest.

**1. Validate the shape of input.** MDN recommends schema validators such as Ajv (a JSON Schema validator) and Zod (a validation library designed for TypeScript, Microsoft's typed superset of JavaScript whose types are checked at build time and removed at run time) and specifically setting `additionalProperties` to false so that keys you did not expect, including `__proto__`, are rejected. A schema also lets you fill in defaults, so the code never falls back to a prototype lookup for a missing setting.

**2. Store user-keyed data in the right structure.** GitHub's CodeQL (a code analysis engine that lets you query source code like a database) query for this bug (`js/prototype-polluting-assignment`) recommends "an associative data structure that is resilient to untrusted key values, such as a Map", or an `Object.create(null)` object. A `Map` stores keys as data, so `"__proto__"` is just a string key.

**3. Read only what you own.** `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` before using an optional setting means a polluted value is never picked up, even if pollution happens elsewhere. This is the gadget-side fix.

**4. Freeze the target.** `Object.freeze(Object.prototype)` makes the shared prototype non-extensible and its properties read-only. MDN calls the broader defence realm lockdown (no changes to any built-in object) and points to SES, a shim (a library that adds a proposed language feature) for Hardened JavaScript; its README says the name stands for "fearless cooperation". SES's lockdown freezes all the shared built-ins, not only one object.

blocks.caption: Freezing turns the pollution into an error (in strict mode; MDN notes it fails silently otherwise). A Map treats __proto__ as an ordinary key.

blocks.md: Freezing has costs. MDN warns that polyfills (code that adds missing built-in features) must run before the freeze, that `Object.freeze` is shallow (other built-in prototypes such as `Array.prototype` stay writable), and that some libraries legitimately modify prototypes and will break. Node.js's `--frozen-intrinsics` flag freezes built-ins for you but is marked experimental. Treat freezing as a strong second layer, tested before production.

blocks.title: Which defence stops which part of the attack

scenes.caption: 2 means the defence blocks that step, 0 means it does not help, 1 means partly. No single row is all 2s: combine a source fix with a gadget fix.
Source-side fixes (first three rows) stop both write routes but do nothing if pollution happens somewhere you did not fix.
Object.hasOwn on the reading side ignores inherited values, so even an unfixed source elsewhere cannot feed this gadget.
Freezing blocks writes to Object.prototype by either route. It scores 1 for gadgets because other prototypes, such as Array.prototype, stay writable unless you lock down everything (SES).
--disable-proto closes only the __proto__ route. Lesson 3's test showed constructor.prototype still polluting with it on.

blocks.md:
**5. Find sources with tools.** CodeQL's `js/prototype-polluting-assignment` traces user-controlled property names into assignments. The ESLint plugin `eslint-plugin-security` (ESLint is the common JavaScript linter) has a rule `detect-object-injection` that flags every `variable[key]` read or write. Most of those are harmless, so teams use it to point reviewers at code rather than to fail builds. Dependency scanners (lesson 12) catch the library side: lodash before 4.17.12, for example, is flagged for CVE-2019-10744.

**6. Test it.** PortSwigger's server-side techniques, such as the Express `json spaces` signal from lesson 4, let you confirm a source without breaking the service. Only test systems you own or are allowed to test: a real gadget can take a shared server down for everyone.

blocks.question: Which pair gives the strongest protection for a settings service that deep-merges JSON from clients and later reads optional settings?
options: --disable-proto=delete and a WAF rule for the string __proto__
Object.freeze on the settings object returned to the client
A schema with additionalProperties false on the input, plus Object.hasOwn (or defaults from the schema) when reading optional settings
Converting the JSON to a string and back before merging
blocks.explain: The schema stops unexpected keys at the source, and own-property reads mean any pollution from another source still cannot feed this code. --disable-proto misses constructor.prototype, a WAF string match is easy to miss with encodings or other routes, freezing the wrong object does nothing, and a JSON round trip keeps __proto__ as a key.

blocks.question: A team adds `Object.freeze(Object.prototype)` to the end of their start-up file. A week later a date-formatting polyfill crashes on import. What happened?
options: The polyfill tried to add a method to a built-in prototype after it was frozen; polyfills must run before the freeze
Object.freeze is recursive, so it froze every module's exports
Frozen objects cannot be read, so the polyfill could not see Object.prototype
Freezing Object.prototype disables the require function
blocks.explain: MDN notes that legitimate prototype modifications such as polyfills must run before freezing. Freezing is shallow, not recursive, and frozen objects remain readable; it only blocks adding or changing properties.

lessons.title: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user

blocks.md:
A **regular expression** (regex) is a small pattern language for matching text. `a+` means "one or more a"; `.` means "any character except a line break"; `( )` groups part of a pattern; `+` or `*` after a group repeats the whole group. Node.js runs regexes with V8's engine, **Irregexp**, which the V8 blog describes as a **backtracking** engine: when the pattern offers a choice, it follows the first option all the way, and if that fails it goes back and tries the next one.

**ReDoS** (Regular expression Denial of Service, OWASP's name) is input that makes such an engine try an enormous number of choices. On Node.js, lesson 1 already told you the stakes: the regex runs on the Event Loop, so while it runs, nobody else is served.

The V8 blog post *An additional non-backtracking RegExp engine* (by Martin Bidlingmaier of the V8 team, January 2021) uses `/(a*)*b/` on the input `aaa`. There is no `b`, so it must fail, but the engine cannot know that the failure is not just a bad choice of how to split the a's between the inner and outer `*`. So it tries every split: `aaa`, then `aa` + `a`, then `a` + `aa`, then `a` + `a` + `a`, and so on. Each extra character roughly doubles the number of splits; the post says `/(a*)*b/` against 100 a's "does not finish within our lifetimes" in Irregexp.

The pattern shape to remember: **a quantifier inside a quantifier** where both can match the same characters.

blocks.title: Ways (a*)* can split the same three characters

scenes.caption: Input: three a's and a character the pattern cannot match. The engine must prove every split fails before it gives up.
Try 1: the inner a* is greedy and takes all three a's as one piece. Then the next character is not b: fail, back up.
Try 2: pieces aa then a. Same characters, different split, same failure.
Try 3: a then aa. Fail again.
Try 4: a, a, a. Three characters already give 4 ways to cut them into non-empty pieces; n characters give 2 to the power (n minus 1). Ten more a's means about a thousand times the work.

blocks.md: The Node.js guide *Don't Block the Event Loop* gives a realistic version: a route that checks a file path with the pattern `(\/.+)+` followed by an end-of-string anchor. In words: "one or more groups of a slash followed by one or more characters, then the end of the string". Because `.` also matches `/`, a string of slashes can be cut into groups in exponentially many ways. The guide's evil input is many slashes followed by a newline, which `.` cannot match, so the whole match must fail. We timed it, adding 4 slashes at a time:

blocks.caption: Every 4 extra characters multiplied the time by about 7. Forty-one bytes of input cost almost two seconds of a server's only JavaScript thread.

blocks.title: Time to reject n slashes plus a newline (measured)

scenes.caption: With 28 or 32 slashes the evil pattern is still fast enough to pass a quick manual test.
Four more characters: 270 ms. Every request to this endpoint now blocks all other users for a quarter of a second.
At 40 slashes, 1.85 seconds. A few such requests per second keep the Event Loop permanently busy: a denial of service from a tiny request.
The rewritten pattern rejects the same 40-character input in 0.005 ms. The bar is too small to see.

blocks.md: **Real case: Cloudflare, 2 July 2019.** Cloudflare, which runs a proxy and content delivery network in front of many websites, pushed a new web application firewall (WAF) rule for detecting XSS at 13:42 UTC. John Graham-Cumming, then Cloudflare's CTO (chief technology officer), wrote in the company's postmortem that the rule "contained a regular expression that backtracked enormously and exhausted CPU used for HTTP/HTTPS serving" on every server, so visitors saw 502 errors for 27 minutes. The WAF was written in Lua (a small scripting language) on PCRE (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions, a backtracking C library) with "no mechanism to protect against a runaway expression"; a protection against excessive regex CPU use had been removed by mistake in a refactoring weeks earlier.

The postmortem's appendix holds a second lesson: **making the quantifiers lazy did not fix it**. Lazy versions (`.*?` instead of `.*`) try short matches first. For the simplified pattern without a trailing semicolon that cut the steps for 20 x's from 555 to 11; but for the variant with a trailing `;`, the lazy form took exactly as many steps as the greedy one: 5,353. Laziness reorders the search; it does not shrink it.

A backtracking regex is dangerous when one string can be matched in many ways: a quantifier inside a quantifier, alternatives that overlap such as `(a|a)*`, or several `.*` in a row. The slow case is the near miss, so a test with matching strings will never show it. On Node.js the cost is paid by every user of the process.

blocks.prompt: A teammate says: "Our regex has nested quantifiers, but I tested it with a 10,000-character valid path and it matched in under a millisecond. So it is safe." Using the Node.js guide, what is missing from that test?
blocks.reveal: A **near miss**. The guide notes that Node.js "generally doesn't have trouble reporting a match even for a vulnerable regexp and a long input string"; the exponential behaviour appears "when there is a mismatch but Node.js can't be certain until it tries many paths". A valid path matches on the first try. The test must include long strings that almost match and then fail at the end, like slashes followed by a newline.

blocks.question: Cloudflare's postmortem compares `.*.*=.*;` with its lazy form `.*?.*?=.*?;` on the input x= followed by 20 x's. What did it find?
options: The lazy form needed 11 steps instead of 5,353
Both needed 5,353 steps: laziness changes the order of the search, not its size, when the match fails
The lazy form could not be compiled by PCRE
The greedy form failed while the lazy form matched
blocks.explain: Graham-Cumming showed that the lazy version of the semicolon pattern still took 5,353 steps for x= plus 20 x's, the same as the greedy one. Laziness only helped the pattern without the trailing semicolon, where a match exists early.

blocks.question: Why is a 2-second regex match worse on a Node.js server than on a server that runs each request on its own thread?
options: Because V8 cannot run regular expressions on a worker thread
Because Node.js restarts the process whenever a regex exceeds one second
It is not worse: Node.js automatically moves regexes to the Worker Pool
Because Node.js runs every request's JavaScript on one Event Loop, so the match delays all other clients, not just the attacker
blocks.explain: Regex matching is ordinary JavaScript work on the Event Loop. The Worker Pool runs only specific I/O and CPU APIs. A thread-per-request server would lose one thread; a Node.js process loses all its JavaScript capacity for the duration.

lessons.title: Fixing ReDoS: rewrite, bound, change engines, cap the input

blocks.md:
There are four fixes, and they stack.

**1. Rewrite the pattern without ambiguity.** In the slash example, the trouble is that `.` can match `/`, so a slash can belong to the current group or start the next one. The rewrite `(\/[^\/\n]+)+`, anchored at both ends, says a segment is a slash followed by characters that are *not* slashes, so every string can be split only one way. GitHub's CodeQL documentation for its `js/redos` query gives the same advice and another example: in `^_(__|.)+_` (anchored at both ends) the alternative `__` overlaps with two `.` steps, and the fix is `^_(__|[^_])+_`.

**2. Bound the input before matching.** A length check is cheap and turns an exponential worst case into a small constant: in lesson 7, 28 slashes took milliseconds and 40 took nearly two seconds. Validate length first, regex second.

**3. Use a linear-time engine.** Some engines never backtrack and run in time proportional to the input length, at the cost of features such as backreferences (`\1`, "the same text the first group matched"). The Node.js guide suggests node-re2, an npm binding to Google's RE2 engine, but warns it "is not 100% compatible with V8's regexps".

V8 has its own. The 2021 blog post describes an experimental non-backtracking engine with two modes: the flag `--enable-experimental-regexp-engine` adds a non-standard `l` ("linear") flag to regexes, and `--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks` makes V8 fall back to the linear engine after too many backtracks (50,000 by default). Node.js passes V8 flags through, so we tried both on Node.js 22:

blocks.caption: The same evil pattern that took 1.85 s at 40 characters runs in under a millisecond once the fallback engine takes over. Patterns with backreferences cannot use the linear engine at all.

blocks.md: Both V8 modes are experimental, and the blog says the fallback skips patterns with backreferences, lookarounds, large bounded repeats, or the `u` and `i` flags. Treat the flag as a safety net that you test with your own patterns, not as the fix. Rewriting and bounding input are the fixes.

**4. Never build a regex from user input.** `new RegExp(userText)` lets the user write the evil pattern themselves. ESLint's security plugin flags this as `detect-non-literal-regexp`; its sibling `detect-unsafe-regex` flags nested quantifiers in literal patterns. If users need search, escape their text and match it literally (or use `includes`); if they truly need patterns, run them with a linear engine and a length cap.

**Finding the patterns you already have.** CodeQL's `js/redos` and `js/polynomial-redos` queries, ESLint's rule, and the small tools the Node.js guide names (safe-regex, rxxr2) all help. The guide is candid that none of them "will catch all vulnerable regexps", so pair them with a near-miss test for every regex that sees untrusted input.

**Regexes are not the only way to block the loop.** The same guide lists other Event Loop blockers that come from input size:

- **JSON DoS.** `JSON.parse` and `JSON.stringify` are linear, but large: the guide's example parses a 50 MB string in 1.3 seconds. Express's body parser (the body-parser middleware that reads request bodies) defaults to a `limit` of `100kb`, and its README warns against raising it far above that.
- **Synchronous APIs.** `crypto.pbkdf2Sync`, `zlib.inflateSync`, `fs.readFileSync` and `child_process.execSync` block the loop for as long as they take. The guide says they "are not intended for use in the server context".
- **Unbounded loops over input**, such as sorting or nested loops over a user-supplied array, scale with the attacker's chosen size.
- **Uncaught errors.** One `throw` that nothing catches, or an unhandled promise rejection (fatal by default since Node.js 15), stops the whole process for every user. Query parsers make this easy: `?q=a&q=b` arrives as an array, so `req.query.q.trim()` throws. Check types, not just keys.

blocks.title: Two ways to keep a heavy job off the Event Loop

scenes.caption: Before: a 40 ms synchronous job (big JSON body, sync crypto, slow regex) runs on the loop, and every other client waits in line until it ends.
Fix A, reject early: a size check refuses the oversized input in well under a millisecond, and the loop moves on.
Fix B, move unavoidable work: async APIs (pbkdf2 with a callback) or a Worker thread run it elsewhere while the loop keeps serving. Simplified: a worker can also be terminated if it runs too long.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** *Prevent*: rewrite ambiguous patterns, cap input length (body parser limits, field length checks), never compile user input as a regex, keep synchronous APIs out of request paths. *Detect*: ReDoS looks like one process at 100 percent CPU while request volume is normal, latency rising for every endpoint at once, and event-loop delay metrics spiking (Node.js exposes `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay` for this); a CPU profile shows time inside the regex engine. *Respond*: Cloudflare's fix in 2019 was a global kill switch for the WAF at 14:07 UTC, with CPU back to normal by 14:09; for an app, roll back or disable the pattern, then find the triggering requests by matching slow-request logs.

blocks.question: A search endpoint does `new RegExp(req.query.q).test(title)` for each title. Which change removes the ReDoS risk while keeping plain-text search?
options: Escape the user's text so it matches literally, or use title.includes(q), and cap q's length
Wrap the call in try/catch
Add the g flag to the regex
Move the code into an async function
blocks.explain: The user controls the pattern itself, so they can write a catastrophic one. Literal matching removes the pattern language entirely and the cap bounds the cost. try/catch does not stop a slow match (it never throws), flags do not change backtracking, and async functions still run on the Event Loop.

blocks.question: Which statement about V8's experimental linear-time RegExp engine is accurate?
options: It supports every JavaScript regex feature, including backreferences
It is enabled by default in Node.js 22
It makes all regexes faster than Irregexp
With --enable-experimental-regexp-engine, a regex created with the l flag runs only on the linear engine, and patterns it cannot handle throw at construction
blocks.explain: The V8 blog and our test agree: the l flag forces the linear engine and patterns like `(a)\1` throw 'Cannot be executed in linear time'. It is behind experimental flags, and V8 says Irregexp is orders of magnitude faster on common patterns.

lessons.title: eval, new Function and why node:vm is not a sandbox

blocks.md:
Sooner or later someone asks: "can users write small scripts to customise our product?" Plugins, formula fields, rule engines and template helpers all lead to running code you did not write. JavaScript makes the naive version easy: `eval(s)` and `new Function(s)` compile a string into code at run time. If any part of that string comes from a user, the user is writing your program: code injection. Node.js's `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings` flag makes both throw an EvalError. The Node.js CLI documentation adds a detail that matters here: the flag "does not affect the Node.js node:vm module".

So people reach for **node:vm**, a built-in module that compiles and runs code "within V8 Virtual Machine contexts". A **context** is a separate global environment inside the same V8 instance: code in it sees a different global object, so `process` and `require` are simply not defined there. It looks like a sandbox. The first lines of its documentation say otherwise: "The node:vm module is not a security mechanism. Do not use it to run untrusted code."

Why not? Because the walls are made of JavaScript objects, and lesson 2 showed that objects are connected. Any host object you pass into the context brings its prototype chain with it. The `constructor` of a host object leads to the host's `Object` function, and the `constructor` of a function is the host's **`Function`**, which compiles a string into a function that runs in the host's global scope. Here is the textbook demonstration, using a context we created only to share a number:

blocks.caption: Inside the context, process is undefined. One step through the shared object's constructor chain and the same code can see the host's process object, which leads to everything Node.js can do.

blocks.title: How the vm context leaks into the host

scenes.caption: The script runs in a fresh context. Its own global has no process and no require, which is what makes vm look safe.
But the global is the object we passed in, created in the host. Its constructor is the host's Object function, not the context's.
Every function's constructor is Function, so one more step reaches the host's Function constructor.
The host Function compiles strings into code that runs in the host realm, where process and require exist. The boundary was never a security boundary.

blocks.md: **Real case: vm2.** vm2 was the popular npm answer: a library that wrapped node:vm in a network of Proxies (objects that intercept every property access) to stop exactly these walks. In July 2023 its maintainer Patrik Simek marked it discontinued, writing that "we now find ourselves facing an escape so complicated that fixing it seems impossible". The project was revived in late 2025, and its current README is frank: "The sheer number of ways to traverse from one object to another in JavaScript makes building an airtight in-process sandbox extremely difficult", and "New bypasses will likely be discovered in the future". GitHub's advisory database bears that out: it lists dozens of critical sandbox-escape advisories for vm2 published in 2026 alone.

**What to do instead.** Put a real operating-system boundary between untrusted code and your secrets:

- **Do not run it** if a safer feature works: a fixed set of formula functions, a JSON rules language you interpret, or a template language without code execution.
- **isolated-vm**, an npm library that gives access to V8's `Isolate` interface: each isolate has its own heap, so host objects are not reachable by property walks. Its README warns that it is in maintenance mode, that leaked isolated-vm objects are "usually trivial" for an attacker to use as a springboard back into the host, and that it is wise to keep isolates in a different Node.js process from other critical infrastructure.
- **A separate process** with as few rights as possible: its own operating system user, no secrets in its environment, the Node.js permission model (lesson 12) as a seat belt, a container or micro-VM, CPU and memory limits, and no network unless needed.

Inside one process, JavaScript objects are a graph, and any shared object is a path back to the host. node:vm, vm2 and similar tools are useful for running *your own* code in a clean global, never for running someone else's. Untrusted code needs a process, container or VM boundary.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: search code for `vm.runIn`, `new vm.Script`, `vm2`, `eval`, `new Function` and string timers, and ask for each: whose code is this? *Detect*: a Node.js service that suddenly spawns shells, reads files outside its directory, or makes outbound connections it never made before; a sandbox escape always ends in one of these. *Respond*: treat an escape as full code execution as the service's user: rotate every secret the process could read (environment variables, files, cloud metadata credentials) and rebuild the host.

blocks.question: A SaaS (software as a service) product lets customers upload JavaScript 'rules' and runs them with `vm.runInNewContext(rule, { order })`. What is the core problem?
options: runInNewContext is slower than eval
Customers cannot use modern syntax in a vm context
node:vm is documented as not a security mechanism; shared objects such as order lead back to the host's Function constructor and from there to process
The rule cannot read order because contexts share nothing
blocks.explain: The Node.js docs say not to use node:vm for untrusted code. Anything passed in, like order, carries a constructor chain back to the host realm. Use a separate, low-privilege process or a non-code rules format.

blocks.question: Why did vm2's maintainers and README say in-process JavaScript sandboxes keep failing?
options: Because JavaScript has no Proxy feature to intercept access
Because the number of paths between objects (prototype chains, constructors, error objects, symbols, async behaviour) is too large to mediate completely
Because Node.js deliberately breaks vm2 in each release
Because sandboxes only fail on Windows
blocks.explain: The current README lists exactly these routes and states that new bypasses will likely be found. Every shared object is a potential path to the host, which is why isolation has to come from a separate heap or process instead.

lessons.title: child_process: shells, arguments and Windows batch files

blocks.md:
Node.js servers often call other programs: image converters, git, PDF tools, a company script. The built-in `node:child_process` module offers two families:

- **`exec(command)`** takes one string and runs it through a shell (`/bin/sh` on Unix, `cmd.exe` on Windows). The shell splits the string and interprets **metacharacters** such as `;`, `|`, `&`, `$( )` and backticks, which chain or substitute commands.
- **`execFile(file, args)`** and **`spawn(file, args)`** start the program directly with an array of arguments. By default there is no shell, so each array element reaches the program as exactly one argument, whatever characters it contains.

The documentation's warning on `exec` is blunt: "Never pass unsanitized user input to this function. Any input containing shell metacharacters may be used to trigger arbitrary command execution." Here is how that looks in Node.js.

blocks.caption: The shell saw a semicolon and ran a second command. execFile handed the whole string to ls as a file name, which simply does not exist.

blocks.title: exec versus execFile with the same input

scenes.caption: exec builds one string and hands it to the shell. The shell, not your code, decides where commands end.
The shell treats ; as a command separator: it runs ls with one argument, then a second, attacker-chosen command.
execFile skips the shell. ls receives one argument containing the semicolon as an ordinary character; there is no second command.

blocks.md: **No shell is not the end of it: argument injection.** Without a shell the attacker cannot start a new command, but if their value *begins with a dash* the program may read it as an option rather than as data. Most Unix tools accept `--` to mean "end of options; everything after this is data":

blocks.caption: With a harmless option the damage is a version banner. Programs with options that write files or run helpers turn the same mistake into something serious. Put -- before user values, or validate them against an allowlist.

blocks.md:
**Two traps in newer Node.js.** First, passing an argument array *and* `shell: true` brings the shell back: the deprecation notice DEP0190 explains that the values "are not escaped, only space-separated, which can lead to shell injection". Node.js made this a runtime deprecation warning in version 24.

Second, Windows batch files. **Real case: BatBadBut, CVE-2024-27980 (April 2024).** RyotaK, a security engineer at Flatt Security, found that on Windows the API function that starts programs (`CreateProcess`) silently runs `cmd.exe` to execute `.bat` and `.cmd` files, and `cmd.exe` uses different escaping rules (the caret `^`, not the backslash) from the ones language runtimes applied. So `spawn("script.bat", [userValue])` without any shell option could still be injected. RyotaK named it BatBadBut, as a pun: it is about batch files, and it is bad, but not the worst. The same post lists Rust, PHP and Haskell as patching too, while Java declined to fix.

Node.js's security releases of April 2024 fixed it for the 18, 20 and 21 lines in a blunt way: `spawn` and `spawnSync` now refuse `.bat` and `.cmd` files with an `EINVAL` (invalid argument) error unless `shell` is set, and the release notes "strongly advise against" the `--security-revert` escape hatch. The current documentation lists the three ways to run a batch file (spawn with `shell`, which DEP0190 discourages; `exec`; or `spawn("cmd.exe", ["/c", "my.bat"])`) and every one of them goes through `cmd.exe`, so user input passed to a batch file on Windows needs strict validation against an allowlist.

Prefer `execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array and no shell; put `--` before user-supplied values; validate values against an allowlist of expected forms; never combine an array with `shell: true`; and on Windows treat every batch file call as a shell call.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: search for `exec(`, `execSync(`, `shell: true` and template strings near `child_process`; run Node.js with the permission model so that a service that never needs child processes cannot start one (`--permission` without `--allow-child-process`, lesson 12). *Detect*: EDR process trees showing `node` as the parent of `sh`, `bash`, `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe` with unusual command lines, and child commands that contain `;`, `|`, `&` or backticks. *Respond*: capture the parent and child command lines from the EDR or audit log, find the request that produced them, and treat the host as compromised.

blocks.question: Which call is safe from both shell injection and option injection when `name` is untrusted?
options: execFile("convert", ["--", name, "out.png"]) after checking name against an allowed file-name pattern
exec(`convert ${name} out.png`)
spawn("convert", [name, "out.png"], { shell: true })
execFile("convert", [name, "out.png"]) with no other checks
blocks.explain: exec and shell: true both hand the string to a shell (DEP0190: array values are only space-separated). Plain execFile stops shell injection, but a name starting with a dash could become an option. The double dash plus an allowlist check closes both.

blocks.question: A Windows service calls `spawn("build.bat", [branchName])` with no shell option, and the team says injection is impossible because no shell is involved. On a Node.js release with the April 2024 fix, what actually happens?
options: The call works and the argument is safely escaped
Node.js converts the batch file to PowerShell automatically
The call fails with EINVAL; and making it work requires shell: true or cmd.exe, which means user input passes through cmd.exe and must be validated
The call works because batch files never use cmd.exe
blocks.explain: Windows always runs batch files through cmd.exe, which is why CVE-2024-27980 existed. The fix made spawn refuse .bat and .cmd without shell, so the team must choose a cmd.exe route and validate branchName strictly.

lessons.title: Deserialisation in JavaScript: node-serialize to React2Shell

blocks.md:
**Deserialisation** turns bytes from a file or request back into objects. The general danger, in Java and Python as much as JavaScript, is that formats able to describe *types* or *code* let the sender choose what runs while loading.

`JSON.parse` is the safe baseline in JavaScript: it only ever produces plain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null, never functions or class instances. (Lesson 2's caveat stands: it happily creates a key named `__proto__`, so what you do with the result still matters.) Trouble starts when a library promises *more* than JSON: functions, dates, classes, references between objects, promises.

**The classic: node-serialize, CVE-2017-5941.** The npm package node-serialize could serialise JavaScript objects including their functions. The US National Vulnerability Database (NVD) entry says that "untrusted data passed into the unserialize() function can be exploited to achieve arbitrary code execution by passing a JavaScript Object with an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE)". An IIFE is a function expression followed by `()` so that it runs the moment it is evaluated.

The cause is visible in the library's own source. It marks serialised functions with a prefix string, and when unserialising it hands any string carrying that prefix to `eval`:

blocks.caption: eval runs whatever text follows the marker, so a string that defines a function and immediately calls it runs during unserialize(). 0.0.4 is still the latest version on npm: the package was never fixed.

blocks.md:
**React2Shell, CVE-2025-55182 (December 2025).** React is the user-interface library from Meta that most JavaScript front ends use. **React Server Components** run some components on the server, and **Server Functions** (Next.js documents them as Server Actions) let the browser call a server function as if it were local: React encodes the call in its own wire format, called the **Flight** protocol, and the server decodes it back into objects and references.

The React team's advisory of 3 December 2025 says Lachlan Davidson, a security researcher, reported on 29 November that an unauthenticated attacker "could craft a malicious HTTP request to any Server Function endpoint that, when deserialized by React, achieves remote code execution on the server", rated CVSS 10.0. Affected: versions 19.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1 and 19.2.0 of `react-server-dom-webpack`, `-parcel` and `-turbopack`, fixed in 19.0.1, 19.1.2 and 19.2.1; frameworks including Next.js, React Router and Waku shipped them. Even an app with no Server Functions of its own could be vulnerable if it supported Server Components.

**Why it is a JavaScript bug, not just a deserialisation bug.** The Flight format lets one part of a payload refer to a property of another part by name. Datadog Security Labs' (the research team of the monitoring company Datadog) analysis shows the patch in React's `requireModule`: the old code returned `moduleExports[metadata[NAME]]` for any name; the fix returns it only `if (hasOwnProperty.call(moduleExports, metadata[NAME]))`. Without that check, a name such as `constructor` or `__proto__` walked up the prototype chain exactly as in lessons 2 and 9, and public proofs of concept chained such lookups to the `Function` constructor. Datadog calls it "a server-side prototype pollution vulnerability" in that sense.

blocks.title: How an attacker-chosen property name reached Function

nodes.label:
POST to a Server
Function endpoint

code runs as
the server user

scenes.caption: An unauthenticated request reaches any Server Function endpoint. The decoder turns the payload into objects and resolves references between them by property name.
The decoder looked names up with a plain obj[name]. For a name the object does not own, that lookup silently continues up the prototype chain.
Names like constructor reach Object, and Object's constructor is Function: the same walk as the vm escape in lesson 9. Simplified: real exploits chained several references.
Function turns attacker text into code that runs with the server's privileges. No authentication was required.
The fix: resolve a name only if the object owns that property. Inherited names such as constructor now return undefined.

blocks.md: **How fast it went.** Datadog saw scanning begin around 22:00 UTC on 3 December, the day of disclosure, after the first (non-working) public proof of concept; a working one was published on 4 December, and Datadog confirmed exploitation even against a blank app created with `create-next-app`. Google Threat Intelligence Group ([GTIG](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/threat-actors-exploit-react2shell-cve-2025-55182)) reported "widespread exploitation across many threat clusters", from China-nexus espionage groups deploying tunnellers and backdoors to financially motivated actors installing XMRig cryptocurrency miners. CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 5 December 2025 with a due date one week later, and its entry marks use in ransomware campaigns as "Known".

Hosting providers deployed temporary WAF rules, and the React team said plainly: "You should not depend on these to secure your app, and still update immediately." A WAF matches request shapes; the bug was in how valid-looking data was interpreted. Patch the library.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: never use formats or libraries that revive functions or arbitrary types from untrusted input; validate parsed JSON with a strict schema; track framework advisories closely, since one framework bug exposes every app built on it. *Detect*: `npm audit` reports the advisory once your lockfile resolves an affected version; at run time look for the Node.js server process spawning shells or `curl`/`wget`, outbound connections to unknown hosts, and reads of `.env` files, all seen in the exploitation Datadog published. *Respond*: patch, then assume compromise for any exposed, unpatched instance: CISA's entry says to check internet-facing instances for signs of compromise after applying mitigations, and secrets in environment variables should be rotated.

blocks.question: Why does the React fix (`hasOwnProperty.call(moduleExports, name)`) stop the attack even though the payload format did not change?
options: It encrypts the Flight payload
It makes the decoder ignore names that are only reachable through the prototype chain, such as constructor and __proto__, so references cannot climb to Function
It blocks requests that contain the word constructor
It disables Server Functions entirely
blocks.explain: The vulnerability was an inherited lookup with an attacker-chosen name. Restricting lookups to own properties is the same gadget-side fix as lesson 6's Object.hasOwn. Keyword filters would be the fragile alternative the React team did not use.

blocks.question: A team wants to send a 'job' object containing a callback function from one service to another and proposes node-serialize. What should they do instead?
options: Use node-serialize but strip the function marker with a regex
Use eval on the receiving side but inside a try/catch
Base64-encode the serialised object so it cannot be tampered with
Send only data (for example a job type name and JSON parameters), validate it with a schema, and map the type name to code the receiving service already contains
blocks.explain: Code should never travel as data across a trust boundary. An allowlist of job types mapped to local functions gives the same flexibility with no deserialisation of code. Regex stripping is a blocklist, try/catch does not stop code from running, and Base64 is an encoding, not protection.

lessons.title: npm inside the process: one realm, full privileges, a seat belt

blocks.md:
The supply chain course followed malicious packages up to the moment they run: install scripts, typosquatting, maintainer takeovers, and the event-stream case of 2018, where a new maintainer slipped a wallet-stealing dependency into a popular package. This lesson starts where that course stops: **what can a package do once your app has loaded it?**

In Node.js the answer is "everything your app can". Lesson 1 quoted the threat model: dependency code "inherits all the privileges of the execution user". There is also no separation *inside* the process. Every module shares one **realm** (the set of built-in objects such as `Object`, `JSON`, `Array` and the global object), so any module can wrap or replace built-ins that every other module uses. The chalk and debug compromise of September 2025, in the supply chain course, did exactly this in browsers by hooking `fetch`.

blocks.caption: A logging helper read a password parsed by unrelated app code, because both share one JSON object. A real implant would send it elsewhere instead of storing it.

blocks.title: One process, one realm, one set of privileges

nodes.label:
shared realm: JSON, Object,
fetch, globalThis

OS user rights: files, env,
network, processes

scenes.caption: Your code and every package, direct or transitive, are loaded into the same process.
They share one realm. A package that replaces JSON.parse or fetch changes it for your code too, as the demo showed.
And all of them hold the operating system user's full rights. Without extra controls, the deepest transitive dependency can read every file and secret the service can.

blocks.md: **The Node.js permission model.** Since Node.js 20 there is a built-in way to shrink the rights: start with `--permission`, and the process loses access to the file system, child processes, worker threads, native addons, WASI (the WebAssembly System Interface, which lets WebAssembly code use files and other system resources) and the inspector (current docs add network and FFI, the foreign function interface) unless you grant each one with flags such as `--allow-fs-read=<path>`, `--allow-fs-write=<path>` and `--allow-child-process`. It became stable in Node.js 23.5.0 and 22.13.0. A run on Node.js 22 with only the app directory readable:

blocks.caption: Everything not granted fails with ERR_ACCESS_DENIED. --permission-audit (Node.js 25.8 and later) reports the same checks without blocking, which is how you discover what an app really needs before enforcing.

blocks.md: The documentation is explicit that this is a seat belt, not a sandbox: it "does not protect against malicious code", because Node.js trusts the code it runs, and "Malicious code can bypass the permission model". It also notes that fs restrictions cover the `node:fs` module, not every route to the disk (it names `node:sqlite`). Use it to limit the damage of bugs and to make attacks noisier; keep containers and OS users as the real boundary.

**Other in-process layers.** Freezing built-ins (lesson 6) stops a package from silently replacing `JSON.parse` for everyone, at some compatibility cost; Hardened JavaScript (SES) goes further with compartments that receive no ambient authority, and its README says Agoric (a smart-contract platform company) and MetaMask (a cryptocurrency wallet browser extension) rely on it in systems that sandbox third-party plugins and mitigate supply chain attacks. These are serious engineering projects, not flags.

**Keeping the tree patched.** `npm audit` sends a description of your dependency tree to the registry and reports known advisories, exiting non-zero if any are found (`--audit-level` sets the threshold for CI). When the vulnerable package is a transitive dependency whose parent has not updated yet, npm's `overrides` field in your root `package.json` forces a fixed version everywhere in the tree; npm's documentation says overrides are only honoured in the root project.

blocks.caption: Names and versions are placeholders. The override pins a patched transitive dependency until its parent catches up; remove it when it is no longer needed, or it will hold back future fixes.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** *Prevent*: the supply chain controls (lockfiles, `npm ci`, install script policies, provenance) decide what enters; inside, run services with `--permission` and minimal grants, no long-lived secrets in environment variables, and a non-root OS user. *Detect*: `ERR_ACCESS_DENIED` errors in logs are a high-signal alert in production, because a correctly configured app never triggers them; in audit mode, subscribe to the `node:permission-model:*` diagnostics channels and log violations. *Respond*: a malicious package in a running process means everything that process could reach is exposed: rotate secrets and rebuild, as in the supply chain course's playbook.

blocks.question: A team enables `node --permission --allow-fs-read=/app` and concludes that a malicious npm dependency can no longer read `/etc` or start processes. What does the Node.js documentation say about that conclusion?
options: It is correct: the permission model is a complete sandbox
It is wrong only on Windows
It is correct as long as --permission-audit is also set
It is wrong: the permission model is a seat belt for trusted code; malicious code can bypass it, so it limits mistakes and raises noise rather than containing an attacker
blocks.explain: The permissions page says the feature does not protect against malicious code and that such code can bypass it. Audit mode makes enforcement weaker, not stronger. Containment needs OS-level boundaries.

blocks.question: Why could a compromised logging library read passwords that the application parsed in completely unrelated code?
options: Because all modules share one realm, so the library could wrap a built-in such as JSON.parse that the application also calls
Because npm packages are installed as root
Because Node.js logs every JSON.parse call to a shared file
Because the lockfile gave the library access
blocks.explain: Modules in a Node.js process are not isolated from each other: built-ins like JSON and fetch are shared objects, and any module can replace them. This is why the threat model treats all loaded code as trusted, and why freezing built-ins is a meaningful hardening step.

lessons.title: Middleware and internal headers: the Next.js bypass

blocks.md:
**SSR** (server-side rendering) means the server runs your front-end framework to produce HTML for each request, instead of sending an empty page that JavaScript fills in. Frameworks that do this, such as Next.js, Nuxt and SvelteKit, blur the line between front end and back end: the same project contains browser code, server code and request-routing code.

**Middleware** is code that runs before a request reaches its page or API handler (Next.js 16 renamed its middleware file convention to `proxy`; the idea and the risk are the same). The Next.js documentation lists uses including rewrites, redirects, adding headers, and authentication and authorisation; the researchers who found CVE-2025-29927 call the last one "the most important". The trap is structural: if middleware is the *only* place a rule is checked, then anything that makes the framework skip middleware skips the rule. Here we look at the mechanism.

**Real case: CVE-2025-29927 (March 2025).** Rachid Allam (zhero) and Yasser Allam (inzo_), two security researchers, found that Next.js used an internal request header, `x-middleware-subrequest`, for a legitimate reason. Vercel's postmortem explains: middleware runs separately from page rendering, and when middleware itself fetches a page of the same app, that inner request must not run the middleware again, or it could loop forever. So the framework marked such subrequests with the header and skipped middleware when it saw enough of them.

The flaw: the header arrived from the internet like any other. The server could not tell its own marker from one a client had typed. In the versions the researchers examined, the check split the header on `:` and counted entries equal to the middleware's name; at `MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH` (5) it returned "continue without middleware". Older versions skipped on a single matching entry. The expected names were easy to guess, so no secret stood in the way.

blocks.caption: The guard itself is reasonable. The bug is that it trusted a header that any client could set.

blocks.title: One internal header skipped the auth check

scenes.caption: Normal request without a session cookie: the server runs middleware first, and the middleware redirects to the login page.
Legitimate use: middleware fetches a page of its own app. The server marks that inner request so middleware does not run on it again.
Attack: a client adds the same header itself. The vulnerable server cannot tell the difference, skips middleware, and serves the protected page.
Patched server: the marker is honoured only with a secret ID generated at start-up, so the forged header is dropped and middleware runs.

blocks.md: **The fix, in Next.js 15.2.3's [source](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/v15.2.3/packages/next/src/server/lib/server-ipc/utils.ts).** When the router server starts it generates 8 random bytes as a hex ID (in `router-server.ts`), and the filter lives in the linked file. Its own subrequests carry that ID in a second header, and a filter deletes `x-middleware-subrequest` from any request whose ID does not match:

blocks.caption: A simplified model of filterInternalHeaders in Next.js 15.2.3 (the real one also strips other internal headers and leaves the ID header in place). An internal signal must be authenticated, here by a secret only the server knows, or stripped at the boundary.

blocks.md: **Timeline and scope.** The researchers reported on 27 February 2025; the Next.js team confirmed it on 14 March, released 14.2.25 on 17 March and 15.2.3 just after midnight GMT on 18 March, made the CVE public on 21 March, and backported 13.5.9 and 12.3.5 on 22 and 23 March. Vercel's postmortem explains the delay (the first report mentioned only old 12.x versions, so it got low priority in triage) and says it should have told other hosting providers sooner. Self-hosted apps using `next start` or `output: 'standalone'` were affected; Vercel-hosted apps were not, because Vercel runs Next.js routing in a separate system, and Netlify and Cloudflare Workers were never affected for the same reason. The advisory's workaround for anyone who could not upgrade: stop external requests carrying `x-middleware-subrequest` from reaching the app.

**The same mistake elsewhere: proxy headers.** Express's `trust proxy` setting decides whether `req.ip`, `req.protocol` and `req.hostname` come from `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host`, headers a reverse proxy adds.
