The [Express guide](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/behind-proxies.html) warns that with `trust proxy` set to `true` the client IP is "the left-most entry" of `X-Forwarded-For`, which a client can write itself, and that the last trusted proxy must remove or overwrite all three headers, "otherwise it may be possible for the client to provide any value". Rate limits, IP allowlists and audit logs built on a spoofable IP are as weak as a skippable middleware. Set `trust proxy` to the exact addresses or number of hops of your own proxies.

Headers that mean something internally (recursion markers, "already authenticated", forwarded client IPs) must either be stripped at the edge or carry proof that only your own infrastructure can produce. And never let one layer be the only authorisation check: Vercel's own advice is not to use middleware as "the sole method of protecting routes".

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: patch; enforce authorisation again where data is read (the Data Access Layer pattern in the next lesson); configure the reverse proxy or CDN to drop internal header names from inbound requests. *Detect*: log and alert on inbound requests carrying `x-middleware-subrequest` or any other internal-only header, and on `X-Forwarded-For` values arriving from addresses that are not your proxies. *Respond*: for a period of exposure, review access logs for protected paths served with 200 to clients that had no valid session.

blocks.question: Why did the fix for CVE-2025-29927 generate a random ID at server start instead of simply removing the recursion check?
options: Because random IDs make the server faster
Because the header was required by HTTP/2
Because the recursion guard is still needed for the server's own subrequests; the ID lets the server prove a marker came from itself, and markers without it are dropped
Because the ID encrypts the response
blocks.explain: The guard prevents middleware from looping on the server's own inner fetches, so it has to stay. What was missing was authentication of the signal. A per-process secret known only to the server separates its own markers from forged ones.

blocks.question: An Express app sets `app.set('trust proxy', true)` and rate-limits login attempts per `req.ip`, but it is reachable directly from the internet as well as through the load balancer. What can an attacker do?
options: Nothing: req.ip always comes from the TCP connection
Send a different X-Forwarded-For value on each request, so every attempt appears to come from a new IP and the rate limit never triggers
Read other users' sessions through X-Forwarded-Host
Force the app to use HTTP/1.0
blocks.explain: With trust proxy set to true, Express takes the left-most X-Forwarded-For entry as the client IP. A client that reaches the app directly, or through a proxy that does not overwrite the header, chooses that value. Trust only your proxies' addresses or hop count.

lessons.title: The server-client boundary: Server Actions, secrets and bundles

blocks.md:
In a full-stack framework one file can hold code for both sides, so it is easy to forget which side a line runs on. Three rules from the Next.js data security guide cover most of what goes wrong.

**1. Every Server Action is a public endpoint.** A Server Action is a function marked `"use server"` that the browser can call. The guide says that once it is created and exported "it is reachable via a direct POST request, not just through your application's UI", even if no page imports it. Next.js gives actions encrypted, non-deterministic IDs that change between builds, but the guide says to "still treat Server Actions as reachable via direct POST requests and verify authentication and authorization inside each one".

blocks.caption: Hiding a button is not access control. The fixed action checks who is calling and whether that user owns this post, which also prevents insecure direct object references (IDOR).

blocks.md:
**2. Know which environment variables reach the browser.** By default Next.js environment variables exist only on the server, but any variable prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is copied into the JavaScript sent to every visitor. A key named `NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_SECRET` is a published secret. The guide recommends that only a **Data Access Layer** (DAL), an internal server-only library that performs authorisation checks and decides what data is returned, should read `process.env` at all.

**3. Mark server-only code.** Importing the `server-only` package at the top of a module causes, in the guide's words, "a build error if the module is imported in the client environment", so a database helper or a key cannot be pulled into a browser bundle by an innocent-looking import. React's experimental taint APIs (`experimental_taintObjectReference` and `experimental_taintUniqueValue`) add a further check that refuses to pass marked objects or values to the client; the guide calls them an additional layer, not a replacement for filtering in the DAL.

blocks.title: What crosses from server to browser

scenes.caption: Secrets live in server environment variables. In the guide's pattern only the Data Access Layer reads them, and it is marked server-only so the build fails if a client module imports it.
Server components receive data from the DAL and render it. Whatever they pass as props is serialised into the page: assume the visitor can read all of it.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are copied into the bundle at build time for every visitor. They must never hold secrets.
Server Actions go the other way: any client can POST to them, with any arguments. So each action calls into the DAL, which authenticates and authorises again.

blocks.md: **Why this matters more than in a classic API.** In a separate front end and back end, everyone knows the API is the boundary. In one SSR codebase the boundary is a string at the top of a file (`"use server"`, `"use client"`) or a variable prefix, and a refactor can move a function across it silently. React2Shell (lesson 11) showed the other half of the risk: the framework's own decoder for those cross-boundary calls is attack surface too, so it must be patched as urgently as any internet-facing server.

Do not treat arguments of a Server Action as typed or trusted because TypeScript declared their types. TypeScript types disappear at run time; the POST body can contain anything. Validate arguments with a schema inside the action, exactly as you would for a REST endpoint.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: a single Data Access Layer that authenticates and authorises every read and mutation; `server-only` on modules that touch secrets; review every `NEXT_PUBLIC_` name; schema validation of action arguments. *Detect*: run a secret scanner over the built JavaScript bundles in CI, not only over source code; log Server Action calls with user IDs so that calls no UI would make, such as deleting another user's post, stand out. *Respond*: a secret that reached a bundle has been published to every visitor and every cache: revoke and rotate it, do not just remove it from the next build.

blocks.question: A developer removes a Server Action from every page, but leaves it exported. Can it still be called?
options: Yes: the guide says exported Server Actions are reachable via a direct POST request even if nothing imports them, so it must still check auth or be removed
No: unused actions are deleted from the server
Only from localhost
Only if the attacker can guess the database schema
blocks.explain: Next.js's data security guide states this directly. Encrypted action IDs raise the bar but are not access control; the guide asks for authentication and authorisation inside every action.

blocks.question: Which environment variable is exposed to every visitor of a Next.js site?
options: DATABASE_URL read only inside a Data Access Layer
NEXT_PUBLIC_MAPS_KEY
SESSION_SECRET read in middleware
API_TOKEN read inside a Server Action
blocks.explain: Next.js inlines variables prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ into client JavaScript. The others stay on the server unless code passes their values to the client explicitly, which is what the DAL and taint APIs help prevent.

lessons.title: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution

blocks.md:
**Electron** builds desktop apps from web technology: it bundles Chromium (the open source browser behind Chrome) with Node.js. It was first built as the application shell for the Atom text editor, under the name Atom Shell, and renamed Electron in April 2015. Chat clients such as Discord and many code editors ship as Electron apps, so the same JavaScript habits now run with desktop powers.

Electron's process model, inherited from Chromium, has two kinds of process:

- **One main process**, the app's entry point. It runs in a full Node.js environment, creates windows, and uses Electron's operating-system APIs (menus, notifications, opening files and URLs).
- **A renderer process per window** (and for embeds), which displays web content and, in the docs' words, "should behave according to web standards". Renderers can be given a full Node.js environment, which "historically ... used to be the default, but this feature was disabled for security reasons".

Electron's security guide states the risk in one sentence: "A cross-site-scripting (XSS) attack is more dangerous if an attacker can jump out of the renderer process and execute code on the user's computer." In a browser, XSS gives the attacker one site's origin. In an Electron renderer with Node.js available, it gives them `require("child_process")`: **RCE** (remote code execution, running commands on the victim's machine from afar).

Three settings in `webPreferences` (the per-window options) decide how far XSS can jump. All three are now safe by default, which is why old apps and apps that turned them off are where bugs live:

- **`nodeIntegration`**: whether page scripts get `require` and Node.js APIs. Off by default since Electron 5.0.0.
- **`contextIsolation`**: whether Electron's internal code and your **preload script** (code that runs in the renderer before the page loads, with access to Node.js APIs) run in a separate JavaScript world from the page. On by default since 12.0.0.
- **`sandbox`**: whether the renderer runs under Chromium's operating-system sandbox, which limits what the process can touch. On by default since 20.0.0.

Context isolation is the subtle one, and it connects straight back to lesson 2. Without it, the page and the preload script share one set of built-ins. The guide explains that with isolation on, "global objects like `Array.prototype.push` or `JSON.parse` cannot be modified by scripts running in the renderer process". Without it, a page script can replace a built-in method, and privileged preload code that later calls that method runs the attacker's version. It is prototype tampering, but the attacker does not need a pollution bug: XSS lets them write to the prototypes directly.

**Real case: Discord desktop RCE (2020).** Masato Kinugawa, a security researcher, reported to Discord's bug bounty a chain of three bugs, published in October 2020:

**Bug 1: missing contextIsolation.** Discord's main window had `nodeIntegration: false` but `contextIsolation` off (the default in that Electron version). Its preload exposed a function that loaded a few allowed native modules, one of which ran an external program through a helper library. By overriding two built-in methods, `RegExp.prototype.test` and `Array.prototype.join`, a page script could change which program that privileged code started.

**Bug 2: XSS in an embed.** Discord showed video embeds in iframes for allowlisted sites. Kinugawa found an XSS on one of them, Sketchfab (a 3D model sharing site), but code in an iframe cannot touch the main page's built-ins.
**Bug 3: a navigation bypass in Electron**, CVE-2020-15174: the `will-navigate` event that apps use to block unexpected navigation was not fired when a cross-site iframe navigated the top-level window. So the iframe could navigate the whole window to the attacker's page, which then ran in the main renderer and used bug 1.

nodes.label:
chat message with
an embed link

program started on
the user's computer

scenes.caption: A message containing a link makes Discord embed an allowlisted site in an iframe. An XSS on that site runs attacker script, but only inside the iframe.
The iframe navigates the top-level window. Electron did not fire will-navigate for this cross-site case, so Discord's navigation check never ran.
The attacker's page now runs in the main window's renderer. With contextIsolation off it shares built-ins with the preload, so it replaces two methods that privileged code uses.

The page calls an exposed function; its privileged code uses the tampered methods and starts a program chosen by the attacker. Any single fix (isolation, iframe sandbox, navigation event) breaks the chain.

blocks.md: **How it was fixed.** Discord first disabled Sketchfab embeds and added the `sandbox` attribute to embed iframes, which stops them from navigating the top window; later it enabled contextIsolation. Sketchfab fixed its XSS, and Electron fixed the navigation event (advisory GHSA-2q4g-w47c-4674; patched in 8.5.1, 9.3.0, 10.0.1 and 11.0.0-beta.1), with the same iframe-sandboxing workaround. Kinugawa reports bounties of USD 5,000 from Discord and USD 300 from Sketchfab. Kinugawa also notes that the built-in-override trick was first found in a 2016 penetration test by the security firm Cure53, which Kinugawa took part in, and led to contextIsolation being added to Electron.

In Electron, every XSS is a candidate for code execution on the user's machine. The defaults (nodeIntegration off, contextIsolation on, sandbox on) are what keep XSS confined to the page; an app that turns any of them off, or runs an old Electron, has removed a wall. Lesson 16 covers the remaining walls you build yourself.

blocks.question: An Electron app keeps `nodeIntegration: false` but sets `contextIsolation: false` so its preload can share variables with the page. Why is that dangerous?
options: It is not: with nodeIntegration off, the page has no access to Node.js
It makes the app ignore its Content Security Policy
It disables HTTPS for remote content
The page shares built-ins with the preload, so injected script can replace methods such as Array.prototype.join that privileged preload code later calls
blocks.explain: This is the first bug in the Discord chain. Without isolation, preload and page share one JavaScript world, so XSS can tamper with built-ins used by code that has Node.js access. Electron's guide says contextIsolation is needed even when nodeIntegration is false.

blocks.question: Which single change would have broken the Discord chain at the navigation step?
options: Raising the bug bounty
Turning nodeIntegration on
Adding the sandbox attribute to the embed iframes, so they cannot navigate the top-level window
Loading the embed over HTTP instead of HTTPS
blocks.explain: Both Discord's interim fix and Electron's advisory workaround were to sandbox iframes. Without the top-level navigation, the iframe's XSS stays inside the iframe, which has no access to the main window's built-ins or preload API.

lessons.title: Hardening Electron: preload, IPC, navigation and fuses

blocks.md: With the defaults on, the page cannot call Node.js. But apps need *some* native features, so they build a bridge: the preload script exposes a small API to the page with Electron's **contextBridge**, and that API talks to the main process over **IPC** (inter-process communication: messages between the renderer and the main process). The bridge is now your attack surface. Electron's context isolation guide shows the classic mistake and the fix:

blocks.caption: From Electron's context isolation and security guides. The bad version lets any script in the page, including XSS, send arbitrary messages to the main process. The good version exposes one fixed action and the main process checks the sending frame.

blocks.md: Why each part matters: a generic `send` turns the bridge into a remote control for every IPC handler you have. Exposing one function per message means injected script can only do what the UI could already do. And the guide explains why the main process must check the sender anyway: "All Web Frames can in theory send IPC messages to the main process, including iframes and child windows in some scenarios". Check `senderFrame.origin` against an allowlist; the guide warns that URLs such as `about:blank` and `blob:` do not identify who controls a frame.

**Navigation and new windows.** The Discord chain needed a navigation. Electron's guide calls navigation "a common attack vector" and recommends blocking it unless needed: a `will-navigate` handler that calls `event.preventDefault()` for any origin outside an allowlist, parsed with Node.js's URL parser, because "a startsWith('https://example.com') test would let https://example.com.attacker.com through". New windows go through `setWindowOpenHandler`, which should return `{ action: 'deny' }` for anything unexpected.

**Opening links outside the app.** `shell.openExternal(url)` asks the operating system to open a URL with whatever program is registered for its scheme. The guide warns that with untrusted content "it can be leveraged to execute arbitrary commands". Only pass URLs whose parsed scheme is `https:` (and perhaps `mailto:`), from an allowlist.

blocks.caption: Adapted from items 13 to 15 of Electron's security checklist. Parsing with URL and comparing origin or hostname exactly avoids prefix tricks.

blocks.title: Walls between page content and the operating system

scenes.caption: Assume the page can be compromised by XSS. With contextIsolation and sandbox on, its only route to native power is what the preload exposes.
Wall 1: the bridge exposes a few named functions, not a raw IPC sender, so injected script cannot invent new channels or arguments.
Wall 2: each main-process handler checks the sender's origin and validates arguments before acting.
Wall 3: navigation and window creation are allowlisted, so the page cannot load a foreign site into a privileged window or hand an arbitrary URL to the operating system.

blocks.md:
**Fuses: switching off features attackers reuse.** Electron's **fuses** are, in the docs' words, "magic bits" in the Electron binary flipped at package time, before code signing, so the operating system's signature checks stop anyone from flipping them back. Several matter for security:

- **runAsNode**: whether the `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` environment variable turns the signed app binary into a plain Node.js interpreter, which the docs describe as a route for "living off the land" attacks (abusing trusted, already-installed programs).
- **nodeOptions** and **nodeCliInspect**: whether `NODE_OPTIONS` and `--inspect` flags are honoured. The docs say most apps can safely disable both. Recall that `NODE_OPTIONS` was the lever in the Kibana case.
- **embeddedAsarIntegrityValidation**: on macOS and Windows, validate the app's packaged code archive (`app.asar`) when it is loaded, so tampering with the installed files is detected.

**Custom protocols are command lines.** Apps often register a URL scheme such as `myapp://` so links can open them. **CVE-2018-1000006** (January 2018) showed the risk on Windows: Electron apps registered as the default handler for a protocol were vulnerable to remote code execution, however the protocol was registered. Fixes shipped in 1.8.2-beta.5, 1.7.12 and 1.6.17. The workaround shows where the danger lay: append `--` as the last argument when registering the handler, "which prevents Chromium from parsing further options". It is the same end-of-options marker as in lesson 10: text from a link must never be read as options.

Electron's own checklist has 20 items, from "Only load secure content" to "Do not expose Electron APIs to untrusted web content". Start a review there: read every `BrowserWindow` and `webPreferences`, every `exposeInMainWorld`, every `ipcMain.handle` and `ipcMain.on`, every `shell.openExternal`, and the fuse configuration in the build. Electronegativity, a scanner from the security consultancy Doyensec, automated much of this check and is now archived in favour of its successor, ElectroNG.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: keep Electron current (it bundles Chromium and Node.js, so its releases carry their security fixes); keep the three defaults; narrow bridges; validated IPC; allowlisted navigation and external links; a strict CSP for local pages; fuses off for runAsNode, nodeOptions and nodeCliInspect. *Detect*: on endpoints, an Electron app's process starting shells or scripting hosts, or being launched with `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`, `NODE_OPTIONS` or `--inspect`, deserves an EDR alert. *Respond*: ship an update quickly (auto-update is part of your incident response plan) and tell users which versions are affected.

blocks.question: A preload script exposes `runCommand: (name, args) => ipcRenderer.invoke('run', name, args)` and the main handler runs whatever it receives. What is the best redesign?
options: Expose specific functions such as exportPdf(docId), and in the main handler check senderFrame.origin and validate docId before running a fixed program
Keep it but obfuscate the channel name
Move the same handler into the renderer
Turn off contextIsolation so the page can call Node.js directly instead
blocks.explain: The bridge should expose actions, not a general command runner, and the main process must verify both the sender and the arguments. Obfuscation is not access control, renderers should not run commands, and turning off isolation removes a wall rather than adding one.

blocks.question: Why does Electron recommend flipping fuses at package time, before code signing?
options: Because fuses only work in development builds
Because unsigned apps cannot use contextBridge
Because fuses encrypt the app's source code
Because then the operating system's code-signing checks make it hard to flip them back without breaking the signature
blocks.explain: The fuses page explains that flipping them before signing makes the OS (for example Gatekeeper, macOS's code-signing check, or AppLocker, Windows's application control) responsible for ensuring the bits are not changed back. The fuses turn off features like ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE and NODE_OPTIONS that attackers could otherwise reuse.

lessons.title: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice

blocks.md:
You now know the main JavaScript-specific bug classes. This lesson turns them into a review checklist, a tool map and a detection plan.

**Review checklist** (search terms in brackets):

1. Input-controlled keys in writes, merges, set-by-path and parsers (`[key] =`, `merge`, `set(`, `qs`); is every container null-prototype or a `Map`, and does every optional setting use `Object.hasOwn`?
2. Regexes that see user input (`RegExp(`, `.match(`, `.test(`, `.replace(`): nested or overlapping quantifiers, no length cap, user-built patterns.
3. Code from strings (`eval`, `new Function`, `vm.`, `vm2`).
4. Process spawning (`exec`, `shell: true`, `.bat`): array arguments, `--`, allowlists.
5. Deserialisers that revive code or types, and framework advisories (React Server Components, Next.js).
6. Trust boundaries in SSR: middleware as the only check, internal headers, `trust proxy`, `"use server"`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_`.
7. Electron: `webPreferences`, `exposeInMainWorld`, `ipcMain`, `openExternal`, navigation handlers, fuses.

blocks.title: Which tool finds which bug class

scenes.caption: 2 means a dedicated query, rule or feature exists; 1 means partial or indirect; 0 means it does not look for this. Manual review is the only column with no gaps, which is why the checklist comes first.
CodeQL has dedicated queries: js/prototype-polluting-assignment, js/redos and js/polynomial-redos, plus code injection and command injection queries that trace user input into sinks.

The ESLint security plugin is pattern-based: detect-unsafe-regex and detect-non-literal-regexp, detect-eval-with-expression, detect-child-process, detect-object-injection. Fast and noisy; good for pointing reviewers at lines.
npm audit only knows published advisories: it catches lodash's pollution bug or React2Shell in your lockfile, but never a bug in your own code.
DOM Invader runs in Burp's browser and is built for client-side prototype pollution sources and gadgets; it does not look at server code or packages.

blocks.md:
**Detection signals, one place.** Most of these bugs end in the same few observable events, so a small set of detections covers many classes:

- **Process tree**: a Node.js or Electron process starting `sh`, `bash`, `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`, `curl` or `wget` (sinks of pollution gadgets, vm escapes, command injection and React2Shell alike). EDR and Linux audit tooling see this.
- **Event-loop health**: event-loop delay metrics and one process pinned at 100 percent CPU while traffic is normal (ReDoS, JSON DoS).
- **Request content**: `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype` in bodies, query strings and parameter names; internal-only headers such as `x-middleware-subrequest` arriving from the internet.
- **Runtime guardrails**: `ERR_ACCESS_DENIED` from the permission model, `ERR_PROTO_ACCESS` from `--disable-proto=throw`, `EvalError` from `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings`, CSP violation reports from browsers. In a correctly working app these never fire, so each one is worth an alert.

**Responding, JavaScript edition.** Three habits differ from other stacks. *Restart* after any suspected pollution, because the change lives in memory for the life of the process. *Rebuild, do not patch in place* after any code execution, because the attacker ran as the service user and could have changed files or `node_modules`. *Rotate* everything the process could read: environment variables, `.env` files, cloud credentials, npm tokens. React2Shell exploitation reported by Datadog went straight for `.env` files.

One idea runs through the whole course: in JavaScript the boundaries you assume (an object, a context, a module, a header, a renderer) are usually not security boundaries. Real boundaries are processes, operating system users, origins and authenticated messages. Put untrusted input and untrusted code behind one of those, and check permission where the data is used.

**Practise legally.** Test only systems you own or have written permission to test. Free places to practise this course:

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy: prototype pollution](https://portswigger.net/web-security/prototype-pollution), with client-side and server-side labs (including the safe detection techniques from lesson 4), and the full [lab list](https://portswigger.net/web-security/all-labs) for DOM XSS and command injection.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/), a deliberately insecure web shop written in Node.js, Express and Angular that you run locally.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (the new home of picoCTF, created by security experts at Carnegie Mellon University) for broader challenge practice.
- Your own lab: run the code from lessons 3, 7, 9 and 10 on your machine, then apply each fix and watch the output change.

blocks.question: After a confirmed prototype pollution incident on a Node.js API, the team deploys the fixed merge function. Which step must not be skipped?
options: Clearing the browser cache of every user
Restarting every process that ran the vulnerable code, because the polluted Object.prototype persists in memory until the process exits
Rotating the TLS certificate
Reinstalling Node.js
blocks.explain: Fixing the code stops new pollution but does not undo pollution already in a running process's heap. If a gadget reached code execution, rebuild hosts and rotate secrets as well.

blocks.question: Which signal is shared by successful exploitation of a pollution gadget like Kibana's, a node:vm escape, command injection and React2Shell, and is therefore worth a single high-priority detection?
options: A spike in 404 responses
A new npm package appearing in package.json
The Node.js server process starting a shell or download tool such as curl or wget
A CSP violation report
blocks.explain: All four end with attacker-chosen commands, usually through a child process of the Node.js server. EDR or audit rules for node spawning shells catch that last step whatever the entry bug was. The other signals are useful but specific to other bug classes.
